analytic.title: Analysis and Design of Fault-Tolerant Scheduling for Real-Time Tasks on Earth-Observation Satellites

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Fault-tolerant scheduling is an efficient approach to improving the reliability of multiple earth-observing satellites especially in some emergent scenarios such as obtaining photographs on battlefields or earthquake areas. Unfortunately, little work has been done to deal with the fault-tolerant scheduling on satellites. To address this issue, this paper presents a novel dynamic fault-tolerant scheduling model using primary-backup policy to tolerate one satellite's permanent failure at one time instant. On this basis, we propose a novel fault-tolerant satellite scheduling algorithm named FTSS, in which an overlapping technology is adopted to improve the resource utilization. Besides, the FTSS employs the task merging strategies to further enhance the schedulability. To demonstrate the superiority of our FTSS, we conduct extensive experiments by simulations using realworld satellite parameters from STK to compare FTSS with other baseline algorithms. The experimental results indicate that FTSS efficiently improves the scheduling quality of others and is suitable for fault-tolerant satellite scheduling.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Earth observation satellites (EOSs) are platforms equipped with optical instruments that orbit the Earth to take photographs of specific areas at the request of users [1]. As the number of satellites grows, multiple satellites are commonly designed to operate in a coordinated way to perform a mission, which significantly improves system performance, cost, and survivability compared with the traditional singlesatellite deployments [2]. Noticeably, real-time applications have been developed and deployed on multiple EOSs, in which the correctness depends not only on the logical results (photographs imaged by EOSs), but also on the time instants at which these results are produced. For example, when an earthquake occurs, there is an urgent need for EOSs to obtain the photographs of affected areas in a real-time manner. Generally, the photographs are expected to be acquired within a few hours or even minutes for conducting damage assessment and planning rescue policies in a timely manner. Missing deadlines on getting photographs may greatly affect damage assessment and rescue resulting in catastrophic consequences [3].

Apparently, the aforementioned real-time application must then incorporate inherent high reliability features. Hence, the management and control system of multiple EOSs on the ground must ensure its functional and timing correctness even when faults occur on some EOSs. Consequently, providing fault-tolerant mechanisms for such a system with multiple EOSs is mandatory owing to the critical nature of tasks executing on EOSs. Furthermore, in this real-time applications, the arrival times and count of these earth-observation tasks are uncertain, which greatly intensifies the difficulty of developing effective fault-tolerant mechanisms.

Scheduling has been regarded as an efficient approach to helping yield high performance in satellite imaging. The most obvious difference between satellite scheduling and other scheduling problems is that tasks can only be executed in visible time windows of EOSs [4]. Bianchessi et al. [1] investigated an improved Tabu search algorithm to solve the multisatellite, multi-orbit, and multi-user scheduling problem, and evaluated the quality of the solution with an upper bounding procedure based on column generation algorithm. Frank et al. [5] modeled this problem using a constraint-based language, and adopted a stochastic greedy search algorithm on the basis of a heuristic guidance strategy to find solutions. Soma et al [6]. constructed a mathematical model for multi-satellite scheduling, and developed an optimization approach based on a genetic algorithm. Zufferey et al. [7] employed the best ingredients of the graph coloring techniques to the satellite range scheduling problems, proposing two new algorithms: a Tabu search and an adaptive memory algorithm. Globus et al. [2] analyzed and concluded the problems of satellite scheduling, proposing the evolutionary algorithm to solve the multi-satellite scheduling problems. It should be noted that the aforementioned static scheduling schemes lack the immediate and dynamic response, not being fit for the applications with uncertain arrival times.

In recent years, more and more attention has been drawn towards the dynamic (on-line) scheduling. For example, Wang et al. [8] investigated an approach to solving the dynamic scheduling problem focused on distributed imaging satellites. Billups et al. [9] addressed both static and dynamic scheduling issues and studied several solutions including a greedy dynamic method, genetic algorithms, integer programming based approaches and a graph theory approach. Liao and Yang [10] put forward a nominal planning with rolling horizon and lagrangian relaxation technique and suggested a dynamic policy FAHA to adjust the nominal planning with updated information. However, the above dynamic scheduling schemes were not designed for real-time applications, and thus cannot guarantee the deadlines of real-time tasks.

Traditionally, many EOSs are not permanently in contact with a ground control station. However, it is feasible to transfer command and detect the state quickly by relay satellites, especially in emergency. On this basis, we recently proposed some dynamic scheduling algorithms with task merging techniques for real-time applications [11], [12], which greatly improve the effectiveness of scheduling on EOSs in emergency.

Although many satellite scheduling algorithms have been proposed, to the best of our knowledge, no work focuses on satellite fault-tolerant study untill now. In some relevant fields, e.g., clusters, grids, and other multiple processor systems, fault-tolerant scheduling has been extensively investigated (e.g., [13], [14], [15], [16]). However, these policies are not suitable for fault-tolerant scheduling on EOSs due to the unique features of EOSs. To bridge the gap, we attempt to design and implement novel fault-tolerant scheduling algorithms for real-time tasks on multiple EOSs. Specifically, our approach focuses on aperiodic, independent, real-time tasks and employs the Primary-Backup model (PB, in short) in which primary-backup overlapping, backup-backup overlapping and task merging techniques are considered within the time window constraints.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: We consider a set T = {t 1 , t 2 , ..., t n } of independent realtime tasks that arrive aperiodically with non-preemptive execution. Because the P ¯rimary-B ¯ackup (PB) model is employed in our fault-tolerant scheduling scheme, each task t i has two copies, i.e., its primary copy t P i and backup copy t B i that execute on different satellites. For a given task t i ∈ T , it can be modeled by t i = (a i , d i , rs i ), where a i , d i , and rs i represent t i 's arrival time, deadline, and resolution requirement, respectively. div.head: B. Fault Model
div.p: The fault model described in this paper includes the following assumptions.

• Faults on satellites are transient or permanent, and independent, namely, a fault on one satellite will not affect another satellite. • Since the probability that two satellites failing simultaneously is extremely small, we assume that only one satellite fails at one time instant. The backup copies can be successfully finished if their corresponding primary copies are on the failed satellite. • A fault-detection mechanism is available to detect satellite failures. New tasks will not be allocated to that known failed satellite. In this study, our primary objective is to accommodate as many tasks and then to minimize the observation resolutions of all accepted tasks under timing constraints.

div.head: A. BB Overlapping
div.p: In order to improve the resource utilization, one of our considerations is to employ the backup-backup (i.e., BB) overlapping mechanism in which a backup copy of one task may overlap with backup copies of other tasks. Fig. 2 illustrates two examples of BB overlapping. Examples of BB Overlapping. The red solid pane represents the available opportunities of task t P 1 , the red dashed pane represents the available opportunities of task t B 1 , the blue solid pane represents the available opportunities of task t P 2 , and the blue dashed pane represents the available opportunities of task t B 2 .
We can observe from Fig. 2(a) that t B 1 and t B 2 are able to overlap. The reason is derived from the following four-fold analysis.

• If resources r 1 , r 2 and r 3 do not occur a fault, t P 1 and t P 2 will be finished successfully, and thus t B 1 and t B 2 do not need to be executed any more. Therefore, t B 1 and t B 2 can overlap. • If resource r 1 meets a fault, t P 1 will then fail, so t B 1 has to be executed. According to the assumption in Section IIB, r 2 and r 3 will not fail, thus t P 2 can be successfully finished. Since st B 22 > ft P 23 , after the completion of t P 2 , the time slot occupied by t B 2 will be reclaimed, which will not result in a conflict between t B 1 and t B 2 with respect to execution time. Hence, t B 1 and t B 2 can overlap. • If a fault occurs at resource r 3 , t P 2 cannot be successfully finished, and there is no timing conflict between t B 1 and t B 2 with the explanation as above analysis.

• If resource r 2 encounters a fault, t B 1 and t B 2 cannot be finished. Based on our assumption, r 1 and r 2 can work normally, then t P 1 and t P 2 can be finished successfully, so the overlapping of t B 1 and t B 2 will not affect faulttolerance. div.head: A. Simulation Method and Parameters
div.p: To validate the performance improvements of FTSS, the targets are randomly generated in the area: latitude -30 • ∼60 • and longitude 0∼150 • . The number of targets are 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, respectively. According to extensive literature such as [17], [18], ten sensors on different satellites are considered in this paper. The parameters of the sensors are presented in Table 1, and the orbit models of satellites are obtained from the Satellite Tool Kit (STK), where the parameters with (*) denote the designed values.

• The arrival time of a task is denoted as a i = a i-1 + intervalT ime, where intervalT ime is a random positive real number, uniformly distributed in [a, b], a 0 = 0; • The deadline d i of task t i is described as

div.head: B. Performance Impact of Task Number
div.p: In this experiment, we investigate the performance impact of the number of tasks that increases from 200 to 1200 with steps Fig. 7(a) shows that with the increase of the number of tasks, the guarantee ratios of all algorithms get decreased. This is because in the condition of limited resources, the increase of the number of tasks makes the system workload heavy. Besides, Fig. 7(a) shows that the guarantee ratio of NMNOFTSS is the lowest because neither the overlapping technique nor the task merging strategies are employed in NMNOFTS, which results in a poor resource utilization. On the contrary, FTSS performs best in terms of guarantee ratio. We attribute the result to the adoption of several overlapping techniques in FTSS. In addition, the guarantee ratio of NMFTSS is higher than that of NOFTSS. This is because the constraints of task merging are stricter, which makes the guarantee ratio of NOFTSS a bit lower.

Fig. 7(b) demonstrates that the observation resolutions of the four algorithms increase with the increase of the number of tasks. This is because when the resources are limited, the increase of the number of tasks results in a heavy system workload, which makes the system have to sacrifice observation resolutions for accepting more tasks. It can be found from Fig. 7(b) that when the system workload is light (the task number is less than 400), the observation resolution of FTSS is better than that of NMNOFTSS, which indicates that FTSS can optimize the observation resolution as well as accept more tasks. When the system workload is heavy (the task number is greater than 600), the observation resolution is worse than that of NMNOFTSS. This is due to the fact that FTSS prefers to accept more tasks, and thus the observation resolution degrades inevitably.

The reason is twofold. First, when interval-Time is in [20,40], the system workload is still heavy. When new tasks arrive, most of the previous tasks have not been finished. However, the decrease of the arrival rate makes the system tend to accept more tasks which leads to the rejection of the following tasks because the previously accepted tasks have not been finished. Hence, the guarantee ratios decrease a bit. Second, when tasks arrive rapidly, more time windows of tasks can overlap with others, which produces more opportunities for task overlapping and merging. However, when intervalTime becomes a little greater (the system workload is still heavy), the opportunities for task overlapping and merging become less, and thus all the guarantee ratios descend. In the period of intervalTime increasing from [20,40] to [80,100], the guarantee ratios of all the algorithms increase. This is because the system workload becomes light, and the previous tasks can be finished when new tasks arrive, and thus more tasks can be finished. It is worth noting that the guarantee ratio of FTSS turns out to be higher than those of other algorithms when intervalTime varies. We attribute this result to the fact that FTSS employs task overlapping and merging techniques, which improves the resource utilization and scales the number of tasks down. As a result, FTSS exhibits the best performance in terms of guarantee ratio.

From Fig. 8(b), it is found that the differences among the four algorithms are tiny. The observation resolutions become better with the increase of intervalTime. The reason is that the system that is in light workload can offer better observation resolutions as well as accept more tasks. Additionally, among the four algorithms, NMNOFTSS has the best observation resolutions while the worst guarantee ratio (see Fig. 8(a)). In emergent situations, the system should accept as many tasks as possible within timing constraints, and meanwhile satisfy users' observation resolutions requirements. Although NMNOFTSS has the smallest observation resolution, it makes the system lose many opportunities to execute tasks. On the contrary, as the employment of task overlapping and task merging techniques, FTSS can improve the guarantee ratio without huge impact on the observation resolutions. The difference between FTSS and NMNOFTSS is only 0.065867. This result proves that FTSS also exhibits a good performance in terms of observation resolution.

div.head: D. Performance Impact of Task Deadline
div.p: The objective of this experiment is to investigate the impact of the tasks' deadline on the performance of the four algorithms. The parameter baseDeadline varies from 20 to 70 with an increment of 10. Fig. 9 illustrates the experimental results. Fig. 9(a) demonstrates that the guarantee ratios of the four algorithms show ascending trends with the increase of baseDeadline. The reason is that the deadline of tasks become loose, which increases the available opportunities for tasks, and consequently reduces the execution conflicts between different tasks. So the guarantee ratios increase. Further, when baseDeadline is 20, the guarantee ratio of NMFTSS is a bit higher than that of FTSS. This is because FTSS tends to merge tasks preferentially. However, in the situation of tight deadlines, this characteristic of FTSS causes some tasks to be unable to overlap with others. Thus, the number of accepted tasks decreases. When baseDeadline varies from 30 to 70, the guarantee ratio of FTSS is always higher than that of NMFTSS. This result can be attributed to the fact that despite the aforementioned characteristic of FTSS, the opportunities for task overlapping also increase in the condition that the deadline becomes loose. It should be noted that when the value of baseDeadline is between 50 and 70, NONOFTSS always outperforms NMFTSS and NOFTSS, however being inferior to FTSS. Fig. 9(b) depicts that the observation resolutions of all the algorithms increase a bit at first, and then shows descending trends with the increase of baseDeadline. When the deadline becomes a bit looser, the system is still overloaded. It has to sacrifice some tasks' observation resolutions for accepting more tasks. However, when the deadline becomes further loosened, the system is able to accept more tasks and offer good observation resolutions at the same time. The observation resolution of FTSS is a bit higher than that of NMNOFTSS (the average difference is only 0.014623), but FTSS accepts more tasks than NMNOFTSS, and so is more suitable for scheduling tasks in emergent situations.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: This paper studies the problem of fault-tolerant scheduling for real-time tasks on multiple observation satellites. The faulttolerant capability is obtained by using primary-backup policy. The scheduling objective is to improve real-time tasks' schedulability and optimizing tasks' observation resolutions within the fault-tolerant requirements. To achieve this objective, this paper first builds a scheduling model based on primary-backup policy, and then analyzes the task overlapping conditions on multiple EOSs and the constraints of task merging elaborately. On this basis, we propose a novel fault-tolerant satellite scheduling algorithm called FTSS, which comprehensively considers task overlapping, task merging and task inserting. FTSS can enhance the resource utilization efficiently, and thus improve the system's performance in terms of guarantee ratios and observation resolutions.

The FTSS algorithm is the first of its kind reported in the literature; it comprehensively addresses the issue of faulttolerance, real-time, schedulability, and adaptivity. To evaluate the performance of FTSS, we conduct extensive experiments to compare it with three baseline algorithms. The experimental results indicate that FTSS efficiently improves the scheduling quality of others.

The following issues will be addressed in our future studies: Firstly, we will extend our fault-tolerant scheduling model to tolerate multiple satellites' failures and propose corresponding scheduling algorithms. Secondly, we will take the communication time and task dispatching time into consideration to enhance the accuracy of scheduling. Thirdly, we plan to implement FTSS in a real satellite system to test its performance.

figure.figDesc: Fig.8(a) demonstrates that when the intervalTime increases from [0,20] to[20,40], the guarantee ratios of all the algorithms decrease. The reason is twofold. First, when interval-Time is in [20,40], the system workload is still heavy. When new tasks arrive, most of the previous tasks have not been finished. However, the decrease of the arrival rate makes the system tend to accept more tasks which leads to the rejection of the following tasks because the previously accepted tasks have not been finished. Hence, the guarantee ratios decrease a bit. Second, when tasks arrive rapidly, more time windows of tasks can overlap with others, which produces more opportunities for task overlapping and merging. However, when intervalTime becomes a little greater (the system workload is still heavy), the opportunities for task overlapping and merging become less, and thus all the guarantee ratios descend. In the period of intervalTime increasing from[20,40] to [80,100], the guarantee ratios of all the algorithms increase. This is because the system workload becomes light, and the previous tasks can be finished when new tasks arrive, and thus more tasks can be finished. It is worth noting that the guarantee ratio of FTSS turns out to be higher than those of other algorithms when intervalTime varies.
